cards.title: The Slice-wise Polynomial Space Conjecture for XNLP-hard problems
cards.formal: Is it true that no XNLP-hard parameterized decision problem has a single deterministic algorithm with both worst-case time (n+2)^{f(k)} and working space f(k)(n+2)^c, for any total computable function f:N→N and any absolute constant c? Here k is the parameter, n is the bit length of the ordinary input, and both resource bounds must hold on the same execution. Hardness uses parameterized logspace many-one reductions defined below.
cards.why: Would explain a broad barrier to reducing the memory of parameterized dynamic programming while keeping polynomial time for each fixed parameter, connecting practical table-size tradeoffs with a uniform complexity-class obstruction.
cards.status_note: Read the source’s resource/reduction definitions and the retained Algorithmica conjecture. Later-result searches through 12 September 2026, including 2026 XALP and scheduling classifications, found no resolution of the stated obstruction.

cards.definitions: A parameterized decision problem Q is a subset of {0,1}*×N, with input (x,k), n=|x| and k supplied in binary. XNLP consists of those Q decided by one nondeterministic multitape Turing machine using time g(k)(n+2)^a and working space g(k)log₂(n+2) for some total computable g and constant a, simultaneously on every branch. An input is accepted exactly when some branch accepts; all branches halt within the bound. The input tape is read-only and excluded from working space, which counts visited cells on the fixed finite-alphabet work tapes. A parameterized logspace reduction Q₁≤Q₂ is a deterministic halting transducer mapping (x,k) to (y,k′), preserving the yes/no answer, with k′≤h(k) for a total computable h and space h(k)+C log₂(n+2) for an absolute C. Its output is write-only and is not counted as working space. Q is XNLP-hard when every problem in XNLP has such a reduction to Q. In the conjectured forbidden deterministic algorithm there is no randomness, oracle or advice, and a single program handles all parameters. Constants, including c and the code computing f, are fixed for that program; f may grow arbitrarily fast but must be computable. Using different computable functions in the time and space bounds is equivalent, since one common f can dominate both. Replacing n by n+2 only handles short inputs. Slice-wise polynomial time allows its exponent to depend on k; the conjectured space bound permits dependence on k only in a multiplicative factor.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the simultaneous resource obstruction for every XNLP-hard problem, or refute it by an XNLP-hard problem and one uniform deterministic algorithm satisfying both bounds for explicit computable f and fixed c. A space bound achieved by a different algorithm, a time bound with a superpolynomial exponent in n at fixed k, or a result for only bounded parameter values does not meet the criterion.

cards.title: Near-optimal Max-Cut on random regular graphs at every fixed degree
cards.formal: Under the intended no-overlap-gap hypothesis, does there exist a classical algorithm, polynomial in n and 1/ε, that for every fixed integer d≥3 and every fixed ε∈(0,1) finds a cut with at least (1−ε)MaxCut(G) edges with high probability when G is a random d-regular graph on n vertices? The degree is fixed independently of the desired accuracy; it cannot be required to grow when ε decreases. The source does not fully specify the conditional hypothesis or whether only AMP algorithms are admissible.
cards.why: Would clarify how the geometry of near-optimal cuts controls efficient optimization in sparse random graphs, and provide a sharper classical benchmark for proposed quantum optimization advantages.

cards.definitions: For n>d with nd even, take G uniformly from all simple undirected d-regular graphs on the labeled vertex set [n]. An assignment σ∈{−1,+1}ⁿ defines a cut of size cut_G(σ)=|{{i,j}∈E(G):σᵢ≠σⱼ}|, and MaxCut(G)=max_σ cut_G(σ). The input is the complete adjacency-list representation and an accuracy parameter; the output assigns a sign to each vertex. Accuracy may equivalently be supplied by an integer m≥2 with ε=1/m, avoiding any unlimited-precision numeric input. Polynomial in n and 1/ε means a bound C_d(n+m)^{a_d} for constants independent of n,m; this records the fixed-degree reading of the source. The success probability, over both the graph and internal algorithmic randomness, must tend to 1 as n→∞ through admissible orders, for each fixed d and ε. No guarantee is required on every individual d-regular graph. The overlap of two assignments σ,τ is R(σ,τ)=n^{-1}Σᵢσᵢτᵢ. An overlap-gap condition excludes a fixed interval of overlaps between sufficiently good assignments; its exact thresholds, randomness and coupling conventions form part of a mathematical hypothesis. The paper’s definitions for diluted k-spin systems do not by themselves specify the no-gap hypothesis for this fixed-degree Max-Cut conjecture. AMP means approximate message passing; a precise class of allowed update rules is not supplied in the conjecture.
cards.answer_criterion: Fix the exact no-gap premise and algorithm class intended by the source, then prove or refute that conditional near-optimal approximation claim for every fixed d≥3 with polynomial dependence on n and 1/ε. A theorem only for sufficiently large d depending on ε, a fixed approximation ratio below one, or numerical performance on finitely many graphs does not settle the target.

cards.title: Erdős’s girth conjecture: dense graphs without short cycles
cards.formal: For every integer k≥1, do there exist constants c_k>0 and N_k such that, for every integer n≥N_k, some simple undirected graph G on exactly n vertices has at least c_k n^{1+1/k} edges and contains no cycle of length less than 2k+2? Equivalently, is M_{2k+2}(n)=Ω_k(n^{1+1/k}) for every fixed k, where M_s(n) is the maximum number of edges in an n-vertex graph with no cycle shorter than s?
cards.why: A central extremal graph question with direct consequences for compact routing and graph sparsification: it asks whether the standard density obstruction from short cycles is asymptotically tight at every fixed scale.
cards.status_note: Read the source definitions and routing use, then checked the July 2026 primary discussion and subsequent searches through 12 September 2026. The later spanner result does not resolve the girth conjecture; no further settled k was found.

cards.definitions: A simple undirected graph consists of a finite vertex set and a set of unordered pairs of distinct vertices; loops and repeated edges are not allowed. A cycle of length ℓ≥3 has ℓ distinct vertices and the edges joining them cyclically. The girth is the length of the shortest cycle, and is +∞ for a forest. Thus “girth at least 2k+2” forbids every cycle of lengths 3,…,2k+1, including non-induced cycles. M_s(n) is a maximum over all such graphs on the vertex set {1,…,n}; connectedness, regularity and efficient construction are not required. The quantifier order is ∀k ∃c_k,N_k ∀n≥N_k ∃G. Constants may depend on k, but not on n; k remains fixed as n tends to infinity. The target is the stated constant-factor asymptotic density, not merely n^{1+1/k−o(1)}, nor a claim for an arbitrarily sparse subsequence of n. This at-least-girth convention reproduces the source’s definition.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed existence claim for every fixed integer k, or refute it for at least one fixed k. Refutation means that no positive c_k and threshold N_k work at that k; a construction for only selected k or a smaller exponent does not settle the universal conjecture.

context_blocks.title: The density allowed by excluding cycles
context_blocks.text: Known extremal upper bounds give M_{2k+2}(n)=O_k(n^{1+1/k}). The conjecture asks whether forbidding all these short cycles still permits that many edges up to a constant factor.

context_blocks.title: Equivalent odd and even girth thresholds
context_blocks.text: Using threshold 2k+1 instead of 2k+2 gives an equivalent asymptotic conjecture: a graph has a bipartite subgraph with at least half its edges, and that subgraph has no odd cycles. This equivalence changes neither the exponent nor the fixed-k target.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
